analysis.title: ING Global Outlook 2027: Power play
key_insights: ING's 2027 base case is a benign year: modest growth, slowing inflation and only mildly restrictive policy rates, if energy prices fall and politics, AI investment and central banks line up. A riskier and a bold call are framed as tail scenarios, not house view.
AI investment is expected to ease somewhat in 2027 but spread into grids, power plants and infrastructure. Growth should be less spectacular but broader.

Falling energy prices are the prerequisite for a soft landing. If prices stay high, central banks could be forced to hike more aggressively, and ING notes some of history's biggest stock crashes followed sharp monetary tightening.

US: ING expects one more Fed hike at the December FOMC (fed funds 4.25% end-2026), then a long pause through most of 2027. Wage growth has slowed to 3% YoY and housing is reacting to higher borrowing costs. ING forecasts 2027 US GDP 2.3% and CPI 2.4%.
The Fed hiked in September and signalled at least one more. Markets priced at least three more 25bp moves, but officials skipped October action, so caution has returned to pricing.

Eurozone: October inflation rose to 4% on energy, core 2.5%. ING expects an ECB hike in December, then a hold through 2027 with a possible cut late in the year. 2027 GDP is forecast at 1.2% (about 1% in the narrative).

UK: BoE hiked in early November for the first time since 2023. ING expects another hike in February and cuts before end-2027 (November). UK inflation is forecast near 4.5% in early 2027 on a roughly 30% rise in household utility bills by April.
Japan: BoJ hit its 2% inflation target in October. ING expects 25bp hikes in December and March, taking the policy rate to 1.75%, below the 2.00% summer level the market expects.

China: ING expects 2027 growth of 4.5% (4.6% in 2026), a PBoC 10bp rate cut in mid-2027, and 10-year yields inching toward 1.6%. ING sees asymmetric risk for Chinese government bonds if deflation fears fade.

FX: the dollar has gained since June, when Fed Chair Kevin Warsh set out to restore policy credibility, reversing the debasement trade that had lifted CHF, gold and bitcoin. ING sees EUR/USD offered in a 1.10-15 range for the next four to five months, then recovering toward 1.18 by end-2027.
Long dollar positioning is a worry. European investors have low hedge ratios on US assets, so the dollar could fall sharply on a US policy misstep.

Rates: ING sees US 10-year yields rising toward 5.25-5.50% in early 2027, then falling to 4.50-4.75% as inflation softens and Fed easing expectations return. Euro 10y swaps could pass 4%, while ING thinks the market is too high on an ECB terminal rate above 3%. French spreads are the focus ahead of the April elections, with the biggest retrace potential afterwards.

Oil: ING's base case is Brent averaging $77/bbl in 2027 (2026 average $90), with a surplus building. Persian Gulf supply is back to about 75% of pre-war levels per the macro section, and flows are near pre-war levels per the energy section. Risk premium persists on US-Iran flare-ups.

Gas: Persian Gulf is about 20% of global LNG trade and LNG flows have recovered less than oil, so European gas stays volatile this winter. ING forecasts TTF at an average of EUR48/MWh in 2027, with a bold call for sub-EUR40 before end-2027.

Five 2027 risks: an AI-triggered equity bear market, second-round inflation effects at scale, weather and infrastructure shocks, a geopolitical de-escalation energy dividend, and a worse bond rout with US 10y at 6% and French spreads past 200bp.

AI-meltdown risk: around a third of US growth has come from AI in 2026, and a further 30% equity drawdown would wipe out about $24.5tr of household wealth, concentrated in high earners. The Fed would likely cut sharply.
Trade: base case is global goods trade growing about 3% in 2027. The bold call is an EU-China trade war with EU tariffs up to 50% on sensitive sectors, hitting almost 30% of world goods trade.
Eurozone housing: ING expects a recovery in activity in 2027 with weak affordability. The risky call has bond market stress keeping mortgage rates high.

Politics: US midterms have passed, with Trump facing a Democratic Congress and Stephen Miller named White House Chief of Staff. Elections in France, Italy, Spain, Poland and possibly Germany carry fragmentation risk, with French politics keeping a risk premium in the euro.

sector_views.rationale: Activity recovers in 2027 but affordability stays constrained, with supply limits putting a floor under prices.
AI capex is expected to ease somewhat in 2027 while spreading to infrastructure and adopters. ING flags correction risk as a tail scenario.

macro_indicators.interpretation: One more hike in December, then a long pause, with easing late in 2027.
Upward pressure to 5.25-5.50% in early 2027, then easing to 4.50-4.75% as inflation cools.
Inflation falls as energy base effects drop out.
Solid growth with a K-shaped split between high-income and other households.
Weak wage growth helps keep inflation cooler.
Energy is the main driver, while core inflation stabilised at 2.5%.
Upside surprise, with about half attributable to distorted Irish figures.
A December hike, then a hold and a possible late-2027 cut.
Inflation peaks in 4Q26 at 4.4% and fades through 2027.
A February hike to 4.25%, then cuts before end-2027 (narrative says November).
Higher gas prices lift household utility bills by about 30% by April.
Hikes of 25bp in December and March, below the market's 2.00% expectation.
Growth stabilises, with the official target likely softened to around 4.5%.
Surplus builds in 2027 but risk premium persists.
European gas stays volatile this winter, easing if Persian Gulf LNG normalises.
Range-bound at 1.10-15 near term, then a gentle recovery.

crypto_views: The dollar's gains since June, after Fed Chair Warsh set out to restore policy credibility, reversed the dollar debasement trade that had boosted the Swiss franc, gold and bitcoin.
risk_factors: AI bubble burst: weak enterprise adoption, cheaper models, overcapacity and higher financing costs trigger credit events, with US recession risk.
Second-round inflation effects: delayed pass-through, tightening jobs markets, oil at $130/bbl or above this winter, and government energy support.
Weather and infrastructure shocks: severe El Niño, low Panama Canal water, or a cyberattack disabling European power, payments or cloud services.
Bond market rout: US 10-year at 6% if growth hits 3-4%, deficits worsen or inflation stays high, stressing leveraged AI players and European public finances.
European political fragmentation ahead of elections in France, Italy, Spain, Poland and possibly Germany.
Fiscal dominance: pressure on central banks to restart asset purchases and cap bond yields.
Dollar drop risk from long positioning, or from an AI bust (IMF estimate: dollar down 6%).
EU-China trade war, and tighter foreign-ownership rules breaking corporate structures.
vol_and_positioning: Long dollar positioning is a worry, and European investors again have low hedge ratios on US assets.
Euro 10-year swaps could pass 4% in a second-round inflation scenario.
US stocks fell on 5 November 2026 as AI and chip stocks sold off, pushing the Nasdaq into correction territory (per a chart caption).
In the AI bust scenario, a 30% further equity drawdown would wipe out about $24.5tr of household wealth.
French spreads could blow out beyond 200bp in the bond-rout scenario, spilling over into Italian BTPs.
geopolitical: US and Israeli strikes on Iran led to the largest oil supply disruption in modern times, with no US-Iran deal yet.
US midterm results leave Trump facing a Democratic Congress, with Stephen Miller named White House Chief of Staff.
Risky call: Iran hawks push Trump toward regime change in Iran and he demands NATO involvement, with tariffs on members that refuse.
De-escalation scenario: a US-driven Ukraine settlement with sanctions relief for Russia, and wider Middle East diplomacy including a settlement with Iran.

UAE has left OPEC, and ING flags Venezuela and possibly Persian Gulf producers or Iraq as exit candidates. The US has growing influence over Venezuelan oil after the capture of President Maduro at the start of 2026.
Elections in France, Italy, Spain, Poland and possibly Germany in 2027 carry fragmentation risk, with French presidential elections in April.
Bold call: an EU-China trade war with EU tariffs up to 50% and mandatory 50:50 joint ventures for Chinese firms in strategic sectors.
UK risky call: PM Andy Burnham calls a snap election, with a bold call that the UK joins an EU customs union.
cross_bank_references: IMF estimates the dollar could fall 6% in an AI bust scenario.

tension_points.bull_case: AI capex eases but spreads into infrastructure and adoption, so growth is broader. The bold call has AI productivity lifting US growth to 5% in 2027, with Treasury yields falling and equities at new highs.
tension_points.bear_case: Weak enterprise adoption, cheaper models and overcapacity trigger credit events. Around a third of US growth has come from AI in 2026, and a further 30% drawdown would wipe out $24.5tr of household wealth.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Weak AI demand, credit events outside the major hyperscalers, or the Fed ceasing to view policy as restrictive.

tension_points.bull_case: Brent falls toward $77 and TTF eases, so second-round effects stay contained and the ECB and BoE cut late in 2027.
tension_points.bear_case: Oil at $130/bbl or above, tighter labour markets and government support lead to more hikes and delayed cuts.
tension_points.what_invalidates: January inflation data and the April CPI report released in May (UK) showing broadening into underlying prices.

tension_points.bull_case: The dollar stays supported until spring by strong US growth, high inflation and a hawkish Fed.
tension_points.bear_case: Long dollar positioning and low European hedge ratios could drive a sharp fall on a US policy misstep. Overseas growth surprises or an AI bust would also weigh.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Energy-driven base effects dropping out of headline inflation in the second quarter, pulling short-dated US rates lower.
